message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure, Harbourside Hotel

## Overall verdict

The basic case that Harbourside is underpriced against its competitive set is plausible, and a rate increase may well be right. But the three claims the author relies on most don't hold up:

1. **The price-sensitivity "test" shows the seasonal pattern, not guests' response to price.**
2. **The £204,000 is not a floor.** It uses the wrong room count, applies the increase to rooms that won't pay BAR, and counts none of the downside risks.
3. **The two-night minimum is aimed directly at 38% of Saturday business**, the wedding guests, and the paper doesn't address this.

## Major issues

### 1. The June→July "test" shows seasonality, not price insensitivity

The paper treats the rise in weekend occupancy from 81% in June to 89% in July as evidence that guests absorbed the £10 increase. Table 1 and its own commentary give a different explanation: "July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays." Occupancy goes on rising into August (93%), then falls back.

- July would very likely have been higher than June **with or without the rate change**.
- The increase came in the last week of June. A large share of July weekend bookings will have been made **before** that, at £135.
- A valid comparison would set July–December 2025 against the same months in 2024, adjusted for any market-wide trend. The paper doesn't show 2024 data.

Not much can be concluded about price sensitivity from this test. The conclusion that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning as a quality option" has no support.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 doesn't help much either. It was earned at a price £20–£35 below competitors. Raising the price may well bring that score down, so it doesn't show guests will accept the higher rate.

### 2. The revenue estimate overstates the gain, so it isn't a floor

**Room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124**.

| | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| As stated | 124 rooms × 104 nights × 79% × £20 | **£203,757** |
| Corrected room count | 112 rooms × 104 nights × 79% × £20 | **£184,038** |

**Not every occupied room pays BAR.** The £20 is applied to every occupied weekend room. But:
- corporate contracted rates and contracted group rates are honoured (Section 6);
- wedding guests, about 38% of Saturday bookings, book as blocks through the couple and are probably on a negotiated group rate, not BAR;
- packages, loyalty and other discounted rates may not move one-for-one.

**Other deductions.**
- If £145 and £165 include VAT, as UK leisure rates normally do, the hotel keeps about **£16.67** of each £20.
- Bookings through online travel agencies lose commission on the increase too.

Here is an illustrative case, assuming 25% of weekend room nights are not at BAR, plus VAT:
- 112 × 104 × 79% × 75% × £16.67 ≈ **£115,000**, before OTA commission.

The actual figure depends on the rate mix, which the paper should show. But the realistic starting point looks closer to **£100,000–£150,000** than £204,000. That's before allowing for any fall in occupancy.

**The "floor" only counts the upside.** The author says the estimate is conservative because it leaves out the gain from extra Friday and Sunday nights. But it also leaves out every loss:
- any fall in occupancy caused by price;
- Saturday stays lost to the minimum-stay rule;
- reduced spending on food, drink and other extras from lost guests.

An estimate that includes only the unquantified upside is not a floor.

**Break-even.** Ignoring the rate-mix issues, BAR revenue per available room at £145 and 79% occupancy is about £114.55. At £165, the hotel matches that at about **69.4%** occupancy. So the BAR increase alone pays for itself unless weekend occupancy falls by about 10 points. That's a useful and reassuring figure, and the paper should present it in place of the June–July argument. Lost spending on food and drink would reduce that margin.

### 3. The two-night minimum works against the wedding business

Section 4 says the minimum will turn single Saturday nights into two-night stays. In the next paragraph it says that **38% of Saturday room bookings are wedding guests** who arrive on Saturday afternoon and leave on Sunday morning. Those are exactly the stays the rule would block.

Wedding guests can't move their dates. Many will book at another hotel, and some couples may book their room blocks elsewhere. The paper needs to say whether wedding blocks are exempt. If they are, much less Saturday business would be converted than the paper implies. If they aren't, this is a significant risk to revenue and to the relationship with Quayside Hall.

### 4. A blanket minimum stay is the wrong tool for most Saturdays

The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. On those dates, a minimum stay can increase revenue, because the room sells either way. On the other 21 or so Saturdays, it turns away single-night guests without any guarantee of replacing them.

The paper expects the gain to come "particularly in shoulder months." That has it backwards. In shoulder months demand is weaker, so minimum-stay rules are more likely to lose bookings than to stretch them. The usual practice is to set minimum stays **date by date** on forecast high-demand Saturdays, not all year.

## Other issues

**Competitive position.**
- At £165, Harbourside will be at the **bottom of the competitor range** (£165–£180), level with the cheapest rival, not below it.
- The author's summary still cites being "£20 to £35 below competitors" as support, but that gap closes completely once the change is made.

**Monitoring trigger.**
- A drop of more than five points, measured monthly against 2025, is a reasonable alarm.
- However, 2025 is not a clean comparison: until late June the rate was £135, not £145.
- Once the minimum stay starts, Saturday occupancy should be tracked separately from Friday.
- The trigger should be based on revenue per available room as well as occupancy, since the trade-off is what matters.
- "We will review the rate" should be tied to a specific action, such as reverting or lifting the minimum stay.

**Timing.**
- Weekends in June and July 2026 that were booked before 15 May will stay at £145, so the first year will fall short of a full annual figure.
- Two weeks' notice to online travel agents is short. It's worth checking that rate parity and channel contracts allow it.

**Unsupported statements.**
- "Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023" comes with no data.
- The basis for comparing value-for-money scores across the competitive set isn't stated.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. **Remove the June–July argument.** Replace it with a year-on-year comparison and the break-even occupancy (about 69% for the BAR increase).
2. **Restate the revenue estimate:**
   - use 112 rooms;
   - apply the increase only to the BAR share of room nights;
   - show figures net of VAT and commission;
   - present central and downside cases instead of a "floor."
3. **Exempt wedding and group blocks from the minimum stay**, or drop the blanket rule. Apply the minimum only on forecast sell-out Saturdays.
4. **Quantify the two-night minimum**, or leave it out of the headline case.
5. **Strengthen monitoring:**
   - track revenue per available room as well as occupancy;
   - report Fridays and Saturdays separately;
   - name a specific action if the trigger is hit.

The rate increase on its own looks defensible, and the break-even figure gives it real headroom. As written, though, the evidence doesn't support the paper's claims. The two-night rule in particular needs redesigning before it goes ahead.
